concepts.name: Role of the kernel
concepts.summary: Explain that the kernel manages CPU, memory, and devices on behalf of programs and provides a protected abstraction layer over hardware.

concepts.name: User mode versus kernel mode
concepts.summary: Describe why the CPU runs user code with restricted privileges and kernel code with full privileges, and how this protects the system.

concepts.name: Process as running program
concepts.summary: Distinguish a program on disk from a process, which has its own address space, state, and resources.

concepts.name: Process states
concepts.summary: Recall the main process states (new, ready, running, waiting, terminated) and what causes transitions between them.

concepts.name: System call interface
concepts.summary: Explain that programs request kernel services such as file I/O or process creation through system calls rather than direct hardware access.

concepts.name: Threads within a process
concepts.summary: Explain that a thread is an execution path inside a process sharing its address space while having its own stack and registers.

concepts.name: Files and directories abstraction
concepts.summary: Understand files as named byte sequences organised in a directory tree, hiding physical disk layout.

concepts.name: Virtual memory idea
concepts.summary: Explain that each process sees its own private virtual address space which the OS maps onto physical memory.

misconceptions.text: The operating system is just the graphical desktop and bundled applications.
A process and a program are the same thing.
Threads of the same process have completely separate memory.

concepts.name: Process creation with fork and exec
concepts.summary: Use fork, exec, wait, and exit to create, replace, and reap child processes in a Unix-like system.

concepts.name: Context switch mechanics
concepts.summary: Explain how the kernel saves and restores register state and process control block data to switch the CPU between processes.

concepts.name: Basic CPU scheduling policies
concepts.summary: Apply first-come-first-served, shortest-job-first, and round-robin to a set of jobs and compute waiting and turnaround times.

concepts.name: Interrupts and handlers
concepts.summary: Explain how devices signal the CPU via interrupts and how the handler runs and returns control.

concepts.name: Paging and page tables
concepts.summary: Translate a virtual address into a physical address using page number, offset, and a page table.

concepts.name: File descriptors and open files
concepts.summary: Use file descriptors, including standard streams, redirection, and pipes, and relate them to kernel open-file structures.

concepts.name: Race conditions
concepts.summary: Identify a race condition on shared data between threads and locate the critical section.

concepts.name: Inter-process communication basics
concepts.summary: Describe pipes, signals, and shared memory as ways for processes to exchange data or notifications.

misconceptions.text: fork starts a brand new program in the child process.
A context switch is free and has no performance cost.
Shortest-job-first is always practical because the OS knows each job's run time in advance.

concepts.name: Mutexes and locking discipline
concepts.summary: Protect critical sections with mutexes, choosing between blocking locks and spinlocks and avoiding lock misuse.

concepts.name: Semaphores and condition variables
concepts.summary: Coordinate threads with semaphores and condition variables to solve producer-consumer and readers-writers problems.

concepts.name: Deadlock conditions and handling
concepts.summary: Analyse a system for the four necessary deadlock conditions and compare prevention, avoidance, detection, and recovery.

concepts.name: Demand paging and page faults
concepts.summary: Trace how a page fault is handled and how demand paging, copy-on-write, and swap affect performance.

concepts.name: Page replacement algorithms
concepts.summary: Compare FIFO, LRU, and clock replacement on reference strings and analyse page fault behaviour.

concepts.name: TLB and translation cost
concepts.summary: Analyse how the TLB hit rate affects effective memory access time and why multi-level page tables save space.

concepts.name: Priority and multilevel feedback scheduling
concepts.summary: Analyse priority-based and multilevel feedback schedulers, including starvation, aging, and priority inversion.

concepts.name: File system structures
concepts.summary: Apply inode, directory, and block allocation structures to explain how files are located, linked, and read.

misconceptions.text: Deadlock occurs whenever a program is slow or waits for a lock.
A mutex and a binary semaphore are identical, including ownership semantics.
LRU replacement always gives fewer page faults than FIFO on any reference string.

concepts.name: Multiprocessor scheduling and affinity
concepts.summary: Analyse trade-offs of per-core run queues, load balancing, and CPU affinity on cache locality and fairness.

concepts.name: Memory consistency and atomics
concepts.summary: Explain how atomic instructions and memory ordering enable lock-free structures and why naive code breaks on modern CPUs.

concepts.name: Thrashing and working set
concepts.summary: Diagnose thrashing and evaluate working-set or page-fault-frequency policies for memory allocation.

concepts.name: File system consistency and journaling
concepts.summary: Evaluate journaling, copy-on-write, and fsck approaches for keeping file systems consistent after crashes.

concepts.name: Device drivers and I/O paths
concepts.summary: Trace an I/O request through the VFS, block layer, driver, DMA, and interrupt completion, including top and bottom halves.

concepts.name: Linux process and scheduler internals
concepts.summary: Analyse how Linux represents tasks and uses a fair scheduler with virtual runtime and cgroups to share CPU.

concepts.name: Isolation with namespaces and cgroups
concepts.summary: Evaluate how namespaces and control groups provide process isolation and resource limits without virtualising hardware.

concepts.name: Performance diagnosis with tracing
concepts.summary: Use syscall tracing, profiling, and kernel counters to judge whether a bottleneck is CPU, memory, I/O, or locking.

misconceptions.text: Lock-free code is always faster than lock-based code.
Journaling guarantees no data loss for any application write.
Containers are lightweight virtual machines with their own kernel.

concepts.name: Designing kernel synchronization schemes
concepts.summary: Design synchronization for kernel data structures that balances scalability, latency, and correctness using fine-grained locks, RCU, or per-CPU data.

concepts.name: Evaluating scheduler designs
concepts.summary: Judge scheduler designs against throughput, latency, fairness, and real-time guarantees such as EDF or rate-monotonic analysis.

concepts.name: Virtualization and hypervisor support
concepts.summary: Evaluate how hypervisors use trap-and-emulate, hardware extensions, and nested page tables to share hardware among guest kernels.

concepts.name: Kernel security and isolation design
concepts.summary: Assess mitigations such as ASLR, capabilities, seccomp, and speculative-execution defences, including their performance and coverage limits.

concepts.name: Designing a file system or storage stack
concepts.summary: Create a file system design choosing on-disk layout, caching, and consistency strategy for given workloads and media such as SSDs.

concepts.name: Kernel architecture trade-offs
concepts.summary: Compare monolithic, microkernel, and hybrid structures such as Linux and Windows NT for performance, reliability, and security.

concepts.name: Debugging kernel failures
concepts.summary: Devise a method to diagnose panics, deadlocks, and memory corruption using dumps, tracing, and debuggers in a live or post-mortem kernel.

concepts.name: Memory management subsystem design
concepts.summary: Design memory policies for allocators, NUMA placement, and huge pages that fit specific workloads.

misconceptions.text: Microkernels are always slower and therefore never used in practice.
Hardware virtualization removes any need for the host kernel to manage guest memory.
Fine-grained locking always improves scalability over coarse locking.
